speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I'm Dr. Agent. Can you tell me how long you've had this painful ulcer on your leg, and have you noticed any changes in its size or appearance since it first appeared?

speaker: Patient
text: 54-year-old woman. The patient reports a skin lesion on her right leg that has been present for 1 month. The lesion began as a small red spot and has increased in size. She recalls an ant bite at the site before the lesion developed. She has a history of anterior uveitis treated with corticosteroids 8 months ago, as well as Crohn's disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypertension.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given your history of Crohn's disease and uveitis, this lesion is highly suggestive of erythema induratum or pyoderma gangrenosum, but I need to rule out other causes. Have you noticed any joint pain, fever, or night sweats, and are you currently taking any immunosuppressive medications for your Crohn's?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Painful ulcerative lesion on the right leg. I also have Lesion has a central necrotic base and purplish irregular borders, History of ant bite at the site of the lesion, Pitting pedal edema of the lower extremities, Dilated tortuous veins in both lower legs.

speaker: Doctor
text: The presence of pitting edema and dilated tortuous veins suggests underlying chronic venous insufficiency, but the painful, purplish, necrotic ulcer with a history of minor trauma is classic for pyoderma gangrenosum, especially given your Crohn's disease. To rule out infection or vasculitis, I need to see the lesion more clearly and check your inflammatory markers. REQUEST IMAGES. text: Given the normal CBC and lack of systemic inflammatory markers, infection is less likely, supporting a diagnosis of pyoderma gangrenosum triggered by the ant bite (pathergy). To confirm the vascular status and rule out arterial disease as a contributing factor, I need to assess blood flow. REQUEST TEST: Ankle-Brachial Index.

speaker: Doctor
text: With normal blood flow ruling out arterial insufficiency and the clinical picture pointing away from infection, this appears to be a case of pyoderma gangrenosum triggered by trauma. I will now perform a biopsy to rule out vasculitis and confirm the diagnosis. REQUEST TEST: Skin Biopsy
